With Claude Ship, announced in beta Monday, “Claude can now review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows,” Anthropic said. The feature is geared toward developers who want to move faster or already delegate a significant amount of coding tasks to agents.

More from ZDNET

“Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person,” Anthropic said. “The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

## How Claude Ship works [...] But Claude Ship isn’t meant for everyone.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” Anthropic said in the release, noting that its own Claude Code team uses Claude to write a majority of the code it needs.

## What Claude Ship means for developers

ZDNET senior contributing editor David Gewirtz said the idea of shipping code at the speed of writing it “raises the hair on the back of my neck.” But he added that, given how impressive Claude Code has been thus far, he wouldn’t be surprised if Anthropic’s deployment tools were equally effective.

Also: Claude Code vs. Codex: Why I use both and how to choose one (if you must) [...] Developer platforms overall are adapting to the new state of the industry. Entire, a GitHub competitor started by the Microsoft-owned platform’s former CEO, is built around the expectation that developers are working side-by-side with agents.

## How to try Claude Ship

Claude Team and Enterprise plan users can try the new feature using the /ship command now available in Claude Code. The feature uses tokens, so your overall bill may change, but it depends on the number of PRs users are putting through Claude Ship — to avoid any surprises, admins can set spending limits for both Code Review and the new PR Steward agent. They can also turn Claude Ship on for an entire repo, meaning developers won’t need the /ship command.

### How Claude Ship works: review, fix, and approve

Claude Ship is made up of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don't have to manage each step manually. [...] # Introducing Claude Ship

Open a pull request and get back to building. Claude can now review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team's policy allows.

Anyone who has opened a pull request knows how this goes. They start on the next thing, and then the review comes back. So they stop, dig back into the old code, push a fix, and wait for the review to run again. Then they go find someone to approve it.

There's a good reason it works this way. Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that's easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too. [...] ## Two ways to get started

### For developers: `/ship` it from Claude Code

Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new `/ship` command in Claude Code. When a change is ready, they run `/ship`. Claude pushes it, opens the PR, reviews the change, and works on feedback and failing checks to help get it ready to merge. What can merge depends on the developer's permissions and the repository's branch rules.

Example of running /ship in Claude Code.

### For admins and engineering leaders: set the rules, one repository at a time

Turning Claude Ship on for an entire repository puts it to work across a team's pull requests automatically, under settings and an approval policy the team controls. Developers don't need to manually invoke the `/ship` command.

# Anthropic's new Claude Ship service hands the reins to agents to fix and review code changes – but the company warns it may 'miss bugs, security vulnerabilities, or other issues'

Anthropic reveals beta tools that let its coding agents automatically approve changes

Nicole Kobie's avatar

Nicole Kobie

Logo and branding of Anthropic's Claude AI tool pictured on a smartphone screen, with branding blending into background.

Follow us

Anthropic has unveiled Claude Ship, claiming the new service will allow agents to review pull requests, fix code problems, and even approve changes.

According to the company, the goal of the new service is to help "ship code as fast as teams write it," while still keeping control of policies. [...] The rise of AI-powered coding has caused issues for developers in recent years, with half saying they don't bother to check AI generated code because it takes longer than reviewing code written by their colleagues.

In a bid to address that, Claude Ship can review pull requests, fix any issues, and then decide using policies whether to merge the change.

"Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that's easy to keep up with when people write every line," the company said in a blog post. "But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too."

"Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person," the company added. [...] ## How Claude Ship works

According to Anthropic, Claude Ship is a combination of its existing Code Review product, as well as two beta agents, PR Steward and Claud Approvals.

Those tools manage code through a process of looking for issues, sorting fixes, looking for further issues, fixing those, and then finally pushing the code through to approval.

Claude Approvals will consider team policies before approving routine changes, with any more challenging or risky changes sent to a human to look over first.

"Code Review performs an in-depth review of pull requests against the codebase through multiple lenses," the company noted. "It collects findings, adversarially verifies them, categorizes them, and posts them to a PR."

results.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes | TechCrunch
results.content:
The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.” [...] Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship, a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes.

The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team. [...] Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.

The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed.

Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.
